Chapter 6: The Moral Limits of Markets
You know, there’s a certain comfort in believing that markets can fix almost any problem. After all, they’re everywhere—whether you’re picking up groceries, hunting for a new place to live, or applying for a job or college. The idea seems straightforward: let people buy and sell what matters to them, and the invisible hand will just sort things out.
But as life gets more complicated, a tough question pops up: Are there some things that money just shouldn’t be able to buy?
Picture a busy city where a new plan is stirring up conversation. The city council is thinking about auctioning off the best seats at public concerts, hoping to raise money for local schools. Some folks are excited, seeing it as a win-win—supporting education while giving eager fans a shot at the front row. But not everyone’s convinced. Should our access to art and culture really come down to who has the deepest pockets?
That uneasy feeling doesn’t stop at concert tickets. Think about hospitals, where some people argue that paying more should mean quicker treatment. Or schools, where parents can’t help but wonder if it’s fair for wealthy families to basically buy their kids’ way into top programs. Suddenly, the logic of the market—so helpful in some places—just feels off in others.
It becomes pretty clear that not everything should be for sale. When money decides who gets a life-saving organ transplant, or who gets a chance to escape a dangerous country, our sense of justice takes a real hit. For most of us, some things are just too important—too closely tied to dignity and equality—to let the highest bidder win.
So, that city debate over concert tickets? It’s really about something much bigger: Where do we draw the line? Some people say markets are neutral—they just show what folks value. But others notice that markets can actually change the meaning of what’s being bought and sold. When things like friendship, love, or even citizenship get treated like products, something special disappears.
One parent, watching all this, remembers a time when neighbors helped each other, no strings attached. That memory sticks—a quiet reminder that not every relationship can, or should, be measured in dollars and cents.
As the city council makes its decision, the community is left with more questions than answers. The market is a powerful tool—no doubt about it. But it can’t solve every question of fairness or justice. Some things are simply priceless. Not because they’re worthless, but because their true value goes far beyond what money can buy.
